title: Triage a slow server
summary: The first five minutes on a sick machine: memory, the cgroup limit, a deleted file that still fills the disk, and strace on a program that will not say why it fails.

steps.title: The first five minutes
body: When a server is "slow" or "broken", seniors run the same short list before they form a theory:
| How long up, how loaded? | `uptime` (load averages over 1, 5, 15 minutes) |
| Which process uses it? | `ps -eo pid,user,comm,%cpu,rss --sort=-rss \\| head` |
| What does a process do right now? | `strace -f -p PID -e trace=file,network` |
| Did the kernel kill something? | `dmesg -T \\| grep -i oom`, `journalctl -k` |
One trap in containers: `free` and `top` show the **host's** memory. The container's own limit is in the cgroup:
`cat /sys/fs/cgroup/memory.max` (bytes), and `memory.current` is what it uses now.

steps.prompt: `df -h /` says the disk is 100% full. `du -xsh /` adds up to only 60% of it. What is the most likely cause?
options: A big file was deleted while a process still has it open, so its space is not freed yet
`du` cannot read files owned by root
steps.explain: A deleted file is only freed when the last process closes it. `du` walks the folders and cannot see it any more; `df` asks the filesystem, which still counts it. `lsof +L1` lists open files with zero links (deleted).

steps.title: Who is using the memory?
prompt: Three programs run on this machine. Find out where the memory goes:
1. `~/answers/top-mem.txt`: the **name** of the process with the most resident memory (RSS).
2. `~/answers/limit-mib.txt`: this container's memory **limit** in MiB, from the cgroup (not from `free`).
3. Stop the memory hog politely, and leave the other two running.

checks.name: top-mem.txt names the hog
checks.fail: That is not the process with the biggest RSS. `ps -eo pid,comm,rss --sort=-rss | head -n5` puts it first.

checks.name: limit-mib.txt is the cgroup limit
checks.fail: The limit is the number in `/sys/fs/cgroup/memory.max` (bytes) divided by 1024 twice. `free -h` shows the host, not this container.

checks.name: the hog is stopped
checks.cmd: for i in 1 2 3 4 5 6; do pgrep -x cache-warmer >/dev/null || exit 0; sleep 0.5; done; exit 1

hints: `ps -eo pid,user,comm,rss --sort=-rss | head -n5`. RSS is in KiB.
`pkill -x cache-warmer` sends SIGTERM to exactly that name.
explain: When a container's memory use reaches `memory.max`, the kernel's OOM killer ends a process inside it, often with
no message in the app's own log. `dmesg -T` (on the host) or `kubectl describe pod` (*OOMKilled*, exit code 137)
shows it. Watching RSS per process and the cgroup's `memory.current` tells you how close you are.

steps.prompt: Match the symptom to the first command you run.
pairs: *No space left on device*, but `df -h` shows free space
A program exits with "startup failed" and nothing else
The service died overnight with no error in its log

steps.title: The disk space that will not come back
prompt: Someone deleted a 40 MB log in `~/var/log/shop` to free space, but the space did not come back. A program still
1. Write the **PID** of the program that holds the deleted file into `~/answers/holder.txt`.
2. Free the space **without stopping that program** (it is a log shipper; restarting it loses its place). Truncate

checks.name: holder.txt has the right PID
checks.fail: That is not the PID that holds the deleted file. `lsof +L1` lists open files with no name left (NLINK 0).

checks.name: the space is freed
checks.fail: The deleted file still holds its 40 MB. Truncate it through the process: `: > /proc/PID/fd/FD` (the FD number is in the `FD` column of `lsof`, like `3w`).

checks.name: log-shipper still runs
checks.fail: `log-shipper` was stopped. The task was to free the space while it keeps running.

hints: `lsof +L1` shows `log-shipp ... 3w ... (deleted)`: the PID is the second column, the file descriptor is `3` (opened for writing).
`: > /proc/$(pgrep -x log-shipper)/fd/3` truncates it to 0 bytes. Check with `lsof +L1` again: SIZE is 0.
explain: On a real server, `rm` on a live log is the usual cause. The proper fixes: truncate instead of deleting
(`truncate -s 0 app.log` or `: > app.log`), use `logrotate` with `copytruncate` or a reload signal, or restart the
program. Writing through `/proc/PID/fd/N` is the emergency move when none of those is possible right now.

steps.title: strace: what is it looking for?
prompt: `~/app/orders-worker` refuses to start and only says `startup failed`. There is no documentation. Find out which
file it wants with `strace`, then create that file so the program prints `orders-worker: ready`. A config with one

checks.name: orders-worker starts
checks.fail: `~/app/orders-worker` still fails. `strace -f -e trace=openat ~/app/orders-worker` shows each file it tries to open; look for `ENOENT`.

hints: `strace -f -e trace=openat ~/app/orders-worker 2>&1 | grep ENOENT` lists the files that were not there. Most are harmless library lookups; one is in your home folder.
It opens `~/.config/orders/worker.ini`. The folder does not exist either.
explain: `strace` shows every system call a program makes, so it answers "what file, what host, what port?" when the
program will not tell you. `-f` follows child processes, `-e trace=file` or `trace=network` narrows the noise, and
`-p PID` attaches to something already running (that needs root or the same user, and is slow, so keep it short in

steps.prompt: An alert says the checkout server is slow. Arrange a sensible first pass, from the broad view to the specific process.
lines: `uptime` and `free -h`: load and memory at a glance
`strace -p PID -e trace=network`: what the busy process is doing
steps.explain: Start wide and cheap, then narrow down. Each step either rules a whole class of causes out or points at the next one. `strace` comes last: it slows the process down and only helps once you know which one to watch.

steps.title: Mission: the disk is full
steps.prompt: Now on a whole machine. In the mission **The disk is full**, do **Where did it all go?** and **The invisible space thief**: find the folder that ate the disk, and the space that `du` cannot see.
steps.explain: `du -xh --max-depth=1 | sort -h` for space you can see, `lsof +L1` for space you cannot: together they solve almost every "disk full" page.

steps.title: Mission: incident night
steps.prompt: One more, with several faults at once. In **Incident night**, do **Triage: what filled the disk?** and **Who's eating the CPU?**.
steps.explain: Real incidents rarely have one cause. Working through the same short list every time keeps you from chasing the first theory.
